extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, and patent agents (UK practice under Patents Acts 1883/1888)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on actions to restrain a patentee's threats, interlocutory injunctions, costs, revocation petitions, and offences under the Patents Acts (principally 1883/1888) as applied in UK courts. Focused on procedural and substantive standards for suing, defending, and seeking revocation of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of validity (31st section) — availability and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A certificate of validity may be given where the patent was established in a case contested in Court; such a certificate may enable the patentee to obtain full costs (including costs as between solicitor and client) in subsequent infringement actions or to have full costs taxed accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show variability: judges have sometimes given the certificate though infringement was not proved (e.g. Automatic Weighing Machine Co. v. ...), sometimes refused; sufficiency of the certificate to direct costs is considered in cases such as Betts v. De Vitre and Bovill v. Hadley. A certificate given in an earlier action may affect costs in subsequent suits but is not available if given after the later action was commenced. See case examples cited (e.g. Glasiam v. Hall; Automatic Weighing Machine Co. v. International Hygienic Society).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability of directors in company infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When directors of a limited company are active parties in an infringement by the company, they may be made parties to a suit against the company and ordered personally to pay the costs of suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Betts v. DC AVENTS and subsequent affirmations; court may pierce corporate veil as to costs where directors take an active part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action under s.32 to restrain patentee's threats — statutory threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person claiming to be patentee, by circulars, advertisements, or otherwise, threatens legal proceedings in respect of alleged manufacture, use, sale, or purchase of the invention, any person aggrieved may bring an action under s.32 for an injunction against continuance of such threats and recover damages if the threatened act was not in fact an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The section does not apply if the person making threats with due diligence commences and prosecutes an action for infringement. Pre-1883 cases required want of good faith; s.32 alters the defence dynamic (see Halscy v. Brotherhood et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of bringing/delaying infringement action (proviso to s.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The section is not to apply if the person making such threats with due diligence commences and prosecutes an action for infringement of his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts interpret 'due diligence' with reference to time when threats were made. An action commenced a reasonable time after threats (e.g. threats in March, action commenced in May) may satisfy due diligence. The infringement action need not be against the aggrieved person but must be bona fide and, to meet some authorities, against a person infringing in the same character as alleged against the threat-plaintiff (Combined Weighing cases; Kekewich J.'s remarks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of mala fides after s.32 — defence available when patentee sues
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Act, absence of mala fides (reasonable and probable cause) is not a complete defence to a threats action unless the patentee has brought and diligently prosecuted an infringement action; otherwise the aggrieved person need only show the threatened act was not infringement (or that patent is invalid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-Act cases required want of good faith; post-Act, the patentee who sues diligently may avoid liability unless mala fides is shown (cases: Sharp v. Brauer; Combined Weighing Co. v. Automatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible proofs in a threats action — non-infringement or invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff in a s.32 action may prove either that he has not infringed any legal right of the defendant, or that the defendant's patent is invalid; in the latter case, the defendant is entitled to the same notice of objections and the same right of beginning and replying at trial as if he had been plaintiff in an action for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invalidity is pleaded, the usual procedural protections and rights in patent validity trials apply (see Kurtz v. Spence and other cited authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome when patentee refuses to sue and trial findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee refuses to bring an action: (a) if the plaintiff shows the patent is invalid or he has not infringed it, he will succeed regardless of the patentee's bona fides; (b) if the patent is shown valid and infringed at trial, the plaintiff in the threat action will fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative authority: Crampton v. Patents Investment Co.; Kurtz v. Spence; cases summarized in the manual's short analytic result list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect where patentee sues for infringement before/after threats action
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee brings an infringement action and (a) succeeds in showing validity and infringement, the action for threats will be decided in his favour; (b) if he fails to establish validity or infringement, he will not be liable in the threat action unless absence of bona fides is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Combined Weighing Machine Co. decisions and Sharp v. Brauer; the patentee's success or good faith litigation conduct materially affects liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a 'threat' under s.32 — examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats may be made by circulars, advertisements, letters from a patentee's solicitor, notices framed to lead people to believe a complainant is alleging infringement, private letters to customers, and possibly 'without prejudice' letters — all may amount to threats under the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Driffield Ac. Co. v. Waterlow; Burt v. Morgan; Kurtz v. Spence; Walker v. Clarke. Advertising a positive statement of infringement pending action may be restrained (Gaulard v. Lindsay). Whether mere warnings of future conduct are 'threats' is doubtful and fact-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction standards in s.32 cases
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory injunction to restrain threats must be moved in the regular way (with notice) and the Court will consider balance of convenience and whether the plaintiff has made out a prima facie case likely to succeed on the questions of infringement and, if raised, validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions have been refused where defendant undertook to proceed with due diligence or where issues overlapped with ongoing infringement actions; interlocutory relief may be stayed until trial of pending infringement actions (see cases: Him* fcoU v. Fairbairn; Combined Weighing decisions; Barney v. United Telephone Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on issuing circulars during pending infringement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff, pending an action he has brought for infringement, has no right to advertise a positive statement that the defendant has infringed; he may be restrained from issuing circulars threatening customers if leave to amend specification by disclaimer has been given but not yet effected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Gaulard v. Lindsay; Fusee Vesta Co. v. Bryant; courts protect defendants/customers from prejudicial circulars while substantive issues remain unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages recoverable in threats actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages (if any) that may have been sustained by the aggrieved person due to the threats may be recovered; when no special damage is proved, nominal damages (e.g. forty shillings) have been awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example authority: Spence, 6 R.P.C. 17; assessment of damages depends on proof of special damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for revocation of a patent (s.26 and prior scire facias grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every ground available previously by scire facias remains available: fraud, non-compliance with conditions (e.g. insufficient specification), invention not patentable (lack of novelty/utility), anticipation (prior art), false suggestion/disconformity between specifications, extension of scope, etc., are grounds for revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative decisions: Gaulard & Gibbs' Patent (disconformity and scope extension); Rex v. Arkwright (insufficient specification); R. v. Cutler (non-patentable invention). The manual lists the historic scire facias grounds as carried forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent comprising more than one invention — not ground for revocation (s.83)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent including more than one invention, contrary to s.83, appears not to be a ground of revocation because that section declares it shall not be competent to take objection on that ground in revocation proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the manual's reading of s.83; practitioners should note limits on raising multiplicity as a revocation ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may present a petition for revocation (standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for revocation may be presented by: (a) the Attorney-General in England or law officers in Scotland/Ireland or persons authorised by them; (b) any person alleging the patent was obtained in fraud of his rights; (c) any person alleging he was the true inventor of an invention included in the patentee's claim; (d) any person alleging public manufacture, use, or sale in the realm prior to the patent date (prior user).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before presenting a petition on the ground of prior user by other persons, authority of a law officer may be necessary. A petition cannot be presented by an agent even if authorised by power of attorney. All persons beneficially interested in the patent must be made respondents. Cases: Walker v. Hydrocarbon Syndicate; Haddan's Patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to deliver particulars of objections in revocation petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with his petition the plaintiff must deliver particulars of his objections to the patent; no evidence will be admitted at trial in proof of any objection not included in such particulars except by leave of the Court or a judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particulars may be amended from time to time by leave. Failure to include an objection in particulars will generally preclude reliance on it at trial without leave (see manual discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rights in revocation proceedings — order of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings at trial are similar to actions where validity is in dispute: the defendant is entitled to begin and give evidence in support of the patent; if the plaintiff gives evidence impeaching validity the defendant is entitled to reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory reference: subsections 5–7 of s.26; parties should expect similar trial conduct and rights as in infringement/validity litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's power to permit amendment by disclaimer and to stay trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court or a judge may, in a revocation proceeding, order that the patentee be at liberty, subject to terms as to costs or otherwise, to apply to the Patent Office for leave to amend his specification by way of disclaimer and may direct the trial or hearing be postponed meanwhile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave to disclaim after presentation of petition has been given on terms such as paying all costs and undertaking to apply forthwith and prosecute with diligence (Gaulard & Gibbs' Patent). The Court can therefore allow remedial amendment subject to conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions attached to leave to disclaim
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to disclaim after presentation of the petition has been granted on terms of the patentee paying all costs and undertaking to apply forthwith for the disclaimer and prosecute the application with diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ganlard & Gibbs' Patent (authority cited). Courts impose costs and diligence undertakings as conditions of allowing later amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assessors and trial without jury in revocation proceedings (s.28)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court may, and on request shall, call in the aid of an assessor specially qualified and try and hear the case wholly or partially with his assistance; the case shall be tried without a jury unless the Court directs otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may request assessors; patent cases are normally non-jury and can involve technically qualified assessors to assist the Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'fraud' in revocation petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing clause (c) (fraud), the word 'fraud' must be confined to grave moral culpability and ought not to be extended to honest mistakes, though the real inventor may have suffered injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Avery's Patent; courts differentiate gross, deliberate fraud from mere errors or innocent misstatements when considering revocation on fraud grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to amend grounds during revocation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A person presenting a petition under some clauses (e.g., fraud, prior user) is entitled after proving his right to present to impeach the patent on any other lawful ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See manual citation: petitioner may expand alleged grounds once right to present established (practical procedural note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy where patent revoked for fraud — Comptroller's power to grant replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent has been revoked on ground of fraud, the Comptroller is authorised, on application of the true inventor made in accordance with the Act, to grant him a patent in lieu of the revoked patent; the new patent is to have the date as the date of the revocation (subject to term limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a statutory remedial route for true inventors displaced by fraudulent patents; parties and advisers should follow the relevant statutory provisions and timing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrar entry and office copy on revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Court has made an order for the revocation of a patent, an office copy of that order must be left at the Patent Office so that an entry may be made in the Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with Patent Office rules (e.g. Court of Patents Rules, 1890) required to record revocation officially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs in revocation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Act of 1883 is silent as to costs, Courts under their general jurisdiction award costs to the petitioner when the patent is revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Haddan's Patent; Edmonds' Patent; practitioners should expect costs to follow revocation in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional and procedural differences (Scotland/Ireland/Isle of Man)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scotland revocation proceedings are in form of action of reduction at instance of Lord Advocate or a party with concurrence; forms and service follow Scottish practice. In Ireland remedies are to be as if patent were granted to extend to Ireland only. There is no provision for service out of jurisdiction in petitions; special procedural orders may be made in cross-jurisdiction situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Drummond's Patent (order nisi allowing trial by affidavit evidence if respondent domiciled in Scotland did not appear). Isle of Man and Scotland have specific prosecutorial and punishment provisions (see s.112, s.108).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence: representing goods as patented when no patent exists (s.105/Act of 1888 summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who represents that any article sold by him is a patented article when no patent has been granted for the same shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine (statute gave up to 5l). Using the words 'patent'/'patented' or similar words stamped, engraved, or otherwise applied to the article constitutes such representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Chravin v. Umber show use of 'Patent' with royal arms on expired patents may disentitle equitable relief; manufacturers advised to add patent number and date to labels to rebut fraud. A provisional specification lodged does not justify use of 'patent' on goods until patent is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence under Merchandise Marks Act 1887 — false trade descriptions as to patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under s.2 of the Merchandise Marks Act 1887, applying a false trade description to goods or selling goods with a false trade description is an offence unless defendant proves innocence. 'Trade description' includes indication that goods are subject of an existing patent; 'false trade description' means materially false as to the goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defences: proving no reason to suspect falsity and giving information about suppliers; penalties can include fine, imprisonment, and forfeiture of articles. Gridley v. Swinborne is an example dealing with expired patents and how the Act may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence: unauthorized use of royal arms in trade (s.106)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who, without authority of Her Majesty or government department, assumes or uses in connection with trade the royal arms (or arms so nearly resembling them as to deceive) in a manner likely to lead others to believe he trades with such authority shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine (statute gave up to 20l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business users of royal arms should be careful not to fall within the section; historical cases emphasize courts will prevent false claims of royal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence: falsely describing oneself as a Patent Agent (Act of 1888)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the first section of the Act of 1888, any person describing himself to be a Patent Agent when he is not on the register is liable on summary conviction to a penalty (statute gave 20l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrations and use of title must comply with the statutory register of patent agents (see Chapter on Institute of Patent Agents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence: false entries in Patent Registers and false copies (s.93)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person makes a false entry in any Register kept under the Act, or a writing falsely purporting to be a copy of an entry, or tenders such writing in evidence knowing it to be false, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties: in the Isle of Man misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment up to two years, with or without hard labour, and fines up to 100l; elsewhere punishments follow general criminal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: International priority under arrangements (s.103) — requirements and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Crown makes arrangements with foreign governments for mutual protection of inventions, a person who has applied for protection in such a foreign state is entitled to a patent under the Act in priority to other applicants with the same date as the foreign application, provided he makes application in this country in the same manner as an ordinary application and within the prescribed months from the date of the foreign application; publication or use in the UK or Isle of Man during that period will not invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The period for filing is statutory (the manual references a months-limit); the provision applies only to foreign states declared by Order in Council. Historical note: Convention of March 20, 1883 (Paris Convention) and list of signatory states provided; practitioners must file within the statutory priority period and follow domestic filing formalities.
